slides.title: The intelligence ladder
slides.caption: When an AI system is not good enough, there are eight things you can change. They are not equally sensible to try.

slides.title: What we will cover
slides.caption: This video covers why the order matters. Then three changes around the AI, five changes to the AI itself, and how to measure.

slides.title: What a model is
slides.caption: At the heart of any AI system is a program that reads text and writes text back. It is called the model.

slides.title: An agent gets a task done
slides.caption: A model on its own only writes answers. An agent is a system built around the model. It lets the model take actions to finish a task.

slides.title: "The model is not good enough"
slides.caption: Saying the model is not good enough does not say what is wrong. It is usually said before anyone has measured what is failing.

slides.title: Training too early costs more than money
slides.caption: Changing the model with new examples is called training. Too early, it wastes money, makes the system heavier and ties you to one model. The real fault stays.

slides.title: The cheap changes keep paying off
slides.caption: Published work shows better wording and better information keep finding gains. Expensive changes often fix something that was never the problem.

slides.title: There are eight things you can change
slides.caption: There are eight things you can change. The first three change the system around the model. The last five change the model itself.

slides.title: Deck A is a ladder
slides.caption: The first three changes run in order, like a ladder. Finish each step before the next one is worth trying. This group is Deck A.

slides.title: Step 1: Instructions
slides.caption: Step 1 is the wording that tells the model the task, called the prompt. Move on when accuracy climbs for a week, then goes flat.

slides.title: Step 2: Context
slides.caption: Step 2 changes what reaches the model, including memory. Move on when it beats a plain version and the failures left are about acting.

slides.title: An agent works in a loop
slides.caption: An agent works in rounds. It picks an action, looks at the result and decides what to do next. This cycle is called the loop.

slides.title: Step 3: Tools and the loop
slides.caption: Step 3 changes the tools and the loop that let the model act. Move on when every round is recorded and what fails is knowing your field.

slides.title: Step 3 is the one most often skipped
slides.caption: Step 3 is the most skipped step. Teams with good context that still fails often jump straight to training.

slides.title: The loop changes the decisions
slides.caption: Changing only the loop changes what an agent decides. Most teams who think they need a trained model need better tools and a better loop.

slides.title: Teach behaviour with examples
slides.caption: Showing the model thousands of tasks paired with good answers teaches it how to behave. This is called fine-tuning.

slides.title: Teach knowledge with raw text
slides.caption: A model first learns by reading huge amounts of text. Letting it keep reading your own documents is called continued pretraining.

slides.title: Behaviour and knowledge are different jobs
slides.caption: Fine-tuning learns behaviour from example pairs. Continued pretraining learns your field from raw text. Each is the wrong tool for the other job.

slides.title: Most companies have lots of raw text
slides.caption: A company with lots of its own documents has raw text but few example pairs. That is why many fine-tuning projects disappoint.

slides.title: Specific facts stay out of the model
slides.caption: Facts about one customer, case or policy stay in documents and the agent's memory. There they can be shown, updated and deleted. A trained model cannot.

slides.title: Deck B is not a ladder
slides.caption: The five model changes do not run in order. Read what is failing, pick the change that fits, and expect to combine them. This group is Deck B.

slides.title: Wrong behaviour? Adapters and fine-tuning
slides.caption: Wrong format, tone or behaviour points to fine-tuning. A small add-on trained on top of the model is called an adapter.

slides.title: Too slow or costly? Distillation
slides.caption: When answers are good but too slow or costly, a large model can teach a smaller, cheaper one. This is called distillation.

slides.title: Wrong judgement? Reinforcement fine-tuning
slides.caption: Right format but wrong judgement points to reinforcement fine-tuning. The model learns from scores. So the results must be checkable.

slides.title: Misreads your field? Continued pretraining
slides.caption: When the model misreads the words, documents or symbols of your field, look at continued pretraining. It lets the model keep reading your text.

slides.title: Data is not text? Custom architecture
slides.caption: When your data is webs of connections, sequences or signals, look at a model built for that data. This is called a custom architecture.

slides.title: Pick by symptom
slides.caption: Read the symptom and go to the matching change: adapters, distillation, reinforcement, continued pretraining or a custom architecture.

slides.title: The options combine
slides.caption: Options combine. Continued pretraining teaches the field, then fine-tuning teaches the task. Distillation can follow any of them.

slides.title: Every step is a measurement
slides.caption: Every decision on the ladder needs a measurement. A fixed set of real cases with known answers is called an evaluation suite.

slides.title: How to build the suite
slides.caption: Build the suite from real failures, before the agent is built. Experts in your field should own it. They know what a correct answer looks like.

slides.title: If the agent remembers, test memory
slides.caption: If the agent keeps memory, test what memory breaks. Try a changed fact, an unanswerable question, a deleted record and someone not allowed to see it.

slides.title: Beats careful people? Treat it as an alarm
slides.caption: A score above careful human performance is an alarm. The system learned to score well without doing the job. Check the scoring first.

slides.title: What this rests on
slides.caption: Deck A rests partly on our own measurements. Deck B comes from published work and vendor documents. The two-deck split is the author's own view.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.caption: Change the system before the model. Climb Deck A in order and pick Deck B by symptom. Behaviour and knowledge need different data. Measure every change.
